item: The boot sweep and the forensics list know the backup route's .oo-backup- snapshot directory, and the route marks it with its owner
summary: A snapshot that a KILL (SIGKILL, power) left in the data folder, a full plaintext copy of the corpus, stayed until someone asked for the next backup, and the forensics inventory counted it as other bytes beside orphaned staging: none found. sweep_stale_backup_temps (run at start and by the maintenance pass) now sweeps .oo-backup-* and judges it by its owner like a streamed backup's .bak-build-* directory: the route writes the one process_owner marker (pid, process start time, host, machine tag) into the directory right after it makes it, so a dead owner's directory goes at the next start at once whatever its age, another live process's stays whatever its age (several servers on one data folder, R176), this process's own is unknown and keeps only the age rule, and a directory with no marker (best-effort write) keeps the 24 h age rule as before. A .restore-* directory is still judged by age alone. The forensics staging list names the prefix and snapshot.db as a plaintext member, so the leftover is reported as a decrypted copy on disk. Measured in a real process: a server killed mid-write left the directory and the marker; the control (marker removed) kept the young directory, with the marker the sweep removed it at once. Eight tests, six mutants (prefix, owner rule, no marker, forensics prefix, forensics plaintext name, owner rule widened to restore dirs) each fail at least one. Stated: the copy stays on disk until the app is next started, because nothing runs in between; a download that outlasted 24 h could be taken by the maintenance sweep (the route already relied on that line). write_owner_marker is the former private _write_owner_marker, renamed because the route now uses it.
